en: The *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra* with its commentary, composed by the excellent scholar Śrī Vāmana.
Now begins the first chapter of the first section.
Having bowed to the supreme light, Vāmana composes this commentary on those *Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtras*, which are dear to poets.
Poetry is to be accepted on account of its ornamentation.
Indeed, poetry becomes something to be grasped and adopted because of its ornamentation (*alaṅkāra*).
This word "poetry" (*kāvyam*) refers to both sound and sense when they are refined by excellences (*guṇas*) and ornaments;
however, here it is taken in a figurative sense to denote sound and sense alone. (1)
To the question "What is this ornament?", he says:
"Beauty is the ornament. (VKal 1.1.2)
*Alaṅkāra* means ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Furthermore, by way of derivation from the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*), this word *alaṅkāra* is applied to similes (*upamā*) and the like. (2)
It [is established] through the removal of defects and the adoption of qualities and ornaments.
Indeed, that ornament must be accomplished by the poet through the abandonment of faults and the acquisition of excellences and ornaments. (3)
According to the treatise, they are as follows.
These [concern] the abandonment of faults and the adoption of qualities and ornaments;
for from this treatise,
having understood [them] through the treatise, one should abandon the faults.
And one should also adopt the poetic qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras). //4//
But what, then, is the fruit of poetry that is adorned with ornaments?
To show that its purpose is this, he says:
"Poetry has both seen and unseen purposes."
Because it is the cause of joy and fame.
Poetry is good; it has a visible purpose because it is a cause of pleasure,
and it has an invisible purpose because it is a cause of fame.
On this matter, there are these verses:
They know that the foundation of a poetic composition is the path to fame;
however, that which leads to infamy is merely a mockery of bad poetry.
The wise say that fame has heaven as its fruit and lasts until the end of time,
whereas infamy is the messenger to the regions of hell devoid of light.
Therefore, in order to acquire fame and to eliminate infamy, the meaning of the *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra* should be clarified by the preeminent among poets. //5//
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Establishment of the Purpose," in the first section, "The Body," of the *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* composed by the illustrious and eminent scholar Vāmana.
Now begins the second chapter of the first section.
[Establishment of the Purpose]
To define the qualified candidate, he says:
"The wise are those who have no relish [for worldly things] and who do not consume even grass. (VKal 1.2.1)
In this world, indeed, two kinds of poets exist:
those who have no appetite for poetry and those who swallow even grass.
The two terms "one who eats raw flesh" (*arocaki*) and "one who consumes grass" (*tṛṇābhyavahārin*) have figurative meanings.
What is that meaning?
It is discernment (*vivekitva*) and non-discernment (*avivekitva*). //1//
As it has been said: "The former disciples [were liberated] because of their discriminative discernment. (Vivekacūḍāmaṇi 1.2.2)
Indeed, in the past, disciples who were disinclined [toward the teaching] were to be instructed because of their discernment and their habit of discrimination. //2//
The others are not so, because they are the opposite of that.
Others who consume their food along with the grass are not disciples;
for they are the opposite of that,
being by nature unable to distinguish [between what is essential and what is not].
And yet, it is not possible to cast off moral discipline. //3//
[Objection: In that case, the scripture would not be beneficial in all instances.
Who, indeed, would think so? To this he says:
"The scripture is not purposeful with regard to non-substances. (VKal 1.2.4)
Indeed, the treatise is not purposeful with regard to non-substances that are indistinguishable [from one another]. //4//
He states an illustration:
"The *kataka* nut is not for the purpose of clearing away mud."
For the kataka nut does not serve to clarify mud in the same way that it does for milk. //5//
Having defined the qualified recipient [of this teaching], he speaks in order to determine the poetic style (rīti):
"Style is the soul of poetry. (VKal 1.2.6)
This so-called *rīti* is the soul of poetry, just as [it is] the body; such is the completion of the sentence. //6//
What, then, is this *rīti*? He says:
*Rīti* is a distinctive arrangement of words (*padaracanā*). (VKal 1.2.7)
Style (rīti) is the composition of words characterized by distinction. //7//
"What is this particularity? he says: "Particularity consists of the qualities. (VKal 1.2.8)
The particularity (*viśeṣa*) consists of the qualities that will be described hereafter. //8//
It is threefold: Vaidarbhī, Gauḍīyā, and Pāñcālī.
And this *rīti* is divided into three types:
Vaidarbhī, Gauḍīyā, and Pāñcālī. //9//
But is it the case that the production of the substance and qualities of poems depends on the influence of place, such that this designation of specific regions is made?
It is not so, as he says:
It is designated by that name because it is observed in Vidarbha and other regions.
The designation [of these styles] is based on their being perceived in their true form by the poets native to Vidarbha, Gauḍa, and Pāñcāla;
however, the regions themselves do not contribute anything at all to the poems. //10//
He states the distinction between them based on the difference in their qualities: "The Vaidarbhī style is endowed with all the [poetic] qualities. (VKal 1.2.11)
The style known as Vaidarbhī is endowed with all the qualities, foremost among which are *ojas* (vigor) and *prasāda* (clarity).
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Not touched by even a trace of defects and woven together with all the qualities," [is the Vaidarbhī].
The Vaidarbha style is desired for its excellence in the beauty of the sounds of the lute.
The wise praise this very [grammar] as follows:
"When there is a speaker, when there is a meaning, and when there is the instruction on words,
that exists without which speech flows forth in vain."

[In this regard] there is an example (Śākuntala 2.6): "Let the buffaloes plunge into the water of the watering-trough, repeatedly struck by their horns; let the herd of deer, gathered in their shadows, practice rumination."
Let the herd of boars confidently root up the musta-grass in the pond, and let this bow of mine find rest with its string slackened. // 11 //
The Gauḍīya style possesses vitality and charm.
That style in which *ojas* (vigour) and *kānti* (splendor) exist is called the Gauḍīyā, characterized by *ojaḥkāntimatī*.
Due to the absence of *mādhurya* (sweetness) and *saukumārya* (tenderness), it abounds in compounds and consists of extremely forceful words.
On this point, there is a verse: [The verse follows]
Those expert in the theory of styles (rīti) sing of the Gauḍīyā style as being endowed with the qualities of vigor (ojas) and luster (kānti), and consisting entirely of most magnificent words.
The example (Mahāvīracarita 1.54):

"The sound of the *ṭaṅkāra* [twang] of the staff-like arm raised to break the staff-like bow of Candraśekhara, which was bent by his staff-like arm, is the drum announcing the commencement of the noble child’s exploits."
How is it that he, whose fierce power is concentrated as he whirls within the belly of the vessel of the universe—its hemispherical halves suddenly overturned—does not even now come to rest? //12//
The Pāñcālī style is endowed with sweetness and delicacy.

The style known as *pāñcālī* is endowed with the qualities of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and delicacy (*saukumārya*). Due to the absence of vigor (*ojas*) and luster (*kānti*), it consists of words that are not strikingly bold and is devoid of brilliance.
And thus says the verse:
Poets know the Pāñcālī style as being sweet and delicate, characterized by a state of loose embrace [of words] yet endowed with an ancient luster.
For example:
"O traveler, in this village no lodging is given to a wayfarer now."
At night, on the floor of the monastery pavilion here, a young traveler fell fast asleep;

by that wicked man, having risen while it was thundering, his beloved was remembered and [an act] was committed such that even today people remain living in fear of the falling of a skull-topped staff.
In these three styles, poetry is established like a painting upon its lines. //13//
Among them, the first should be accepted,
because it possesses the fullness of all qualities.
Among these three styles (rītis), the Vaidarbha is to be adopted first, because of its completeness of qualities (guṇas). //14//
But not the others,
because their qualities are meager.
The other two, Gauḍīyā and Pāñcālī, are not to be adopted, because they are qualities of the *stotra*. //15//
Some say that the practice of the other [limbs] is for the purpose of ascending to that [yoga].
Some maintain that the practice of the other two styles was for the sake of ascending to that very Vaidarbhī style alone. //16//
But that is not so; for one whose conduct is not based on reality does not achieve reality.
For truth does not arise for one who practices what is not true. //17//
He states an illustration:
"By the practice of weaving hemp threads, one does not attain the variety found in weaving silk threads. (VKal 1.2.18)
For indeed, a weaver practicing the weaving of hemp thread does not attain the variety found in the weaving of fine silk thread. //18//
That too, when devoid of compounds, is the pure Vaidarbhī style.
That Vaidarbhi style is called pure Vaidarbhi if it does not contain compounds. //19//
In that [speech], the excellence of the qualities of meaning is to be relished.
In that Vaidarbhī style, there is the relishable quality of the excellence of meaning. //20//
From ascending that [ladder], there is even a slight trace of the quality of meaning.
Indeed, by means of that very support, even a mere fraction of the qualities of the meaning becomes palatable;
how much more so, then,
the perfection of the qualities of the meaning?
And so they have said:
"However, there exists another entirely distinct sequence of words, in which nothing at all appears as if it were something."
And having reached the path of the ears, it gladdens the hearts of the virtuous, as if a rain of nectar has entered within.
Wherein the splendor of expression flows, resting upon the word as its foundation, and wherein the reality of an object passes from unreality to truth—
such a thing indeed arises somewhere within the Vaidarbha style.
It is a certain kind of poetic flavor that delights the hearts of those with sensitive taste. //21//
She too is called Vaidarbhī,
by virtue of residing therein.
This perfection of the qualities of meaning is also called *Vaidarbha*;
by this he shows that the designation is used figuratively (*upacārataḥ*) on account of its presence therein. //22//

Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the consideration of the qualified student and the determination of the *rītis*, in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) titled "The Body" (*śārīra*) of the *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* composed by the illustrious and most excellent scholar Vāmana.
Now begins the third chapter of the first section.
Having examined the considerations regarding the qualified candidate and the nature of literary style, he speaks in order to demonstrate the constituent elements of poetry:
The world, knowledge, and miscellaneous [treatises] are the auxiliary limbs of poetry.
He explains this according to the order of the headings:
"The world's conduct is the world. (VKal 1.3.2)
The world consists of the stationary and the moving; its "vartana" means its mode of existence or conduct. //2//
The sciences preceded by grammar, lexicography, dictionaries, prosody, the arts, erotics, and statecraft. (VKal 1.3.3)
The fact that verbal memory and so forth are preceded by that [perception] is due to their necessity for prior reference in poetic compositions. //3//
In order to establish their status as constituent parts of poetry, he says:
"From the grammatical tradition (śabdasmṛti) comes the purity of words (śabdaśuddhi)."

The purity of words—the determination of their correctness—must be established through grammar by means of the recollection of linguistic forms; for it is only pure words that are employed by poets free from hesitation. (4)
The determination of the meaning of words is derived from a lexicon.

For if one were to contemplate a word as being suitable for entry into a poetic composition while harboring doubt regarding its meaning, one would neither grasp it nor abandon it; thus, there would be an obstacle to the composition of poetry. Therefore, the determination of the meaning of words must be made through a lexicon (*abhidhānakośa*).
However, it is incorrect to claim that the purpose of a lexicon is merely to provide the expression of something previously unknown.
Because that which is not employed cannot be employed.
If that which has already been employed were to be employed again, then why would the ambiguity of meaning (*sandigdhārthatva*) of the word have been suspected?
That is not so; for in that case, the comprehension of the general meaning is possible.
