As he grew with the enjoyment of various foods, the knot of his lower garment,
though previously tied by someone else, became loosened by the protruding bones of his ribs.
Thus is the application [of the term], whether due to error or through metaphorical usage. //5//
The *Chandoviciti* is for the purpose of resolving doubts regarding metrical feet.
Through the practice of poetry, the mastery of meters certainly comes about; however, there may still be doubt regarding certain meters such as those measured by morae (mātrāvṛtta).
Therefore, the purpose of Prosody (Chandovicitih) is to provide the means for resolving doubts concerning meters. //6//
From the arts and sciences arises the consciousness of the principle of art (kalātattva).
The arts (kalā) consist of singing, dancing, painting, and so forth; the treatises composed by Viśākhila and others that designate these are the "treatises on the arts" (kalāśāstra).
From these comes the consciousness—that is, the realization—of the reality of the arts (kalātattva).
For indeed, without the apprehension of the reality of the arts, it is impossible to properly compose a work concerning the subject matter of the arts. //7//
From the science of love (kāmaśāstra), [one learns] the practice of love (kāmopacāra).

The term "knowledge" (saṃvit) carries over [from the previous rule]. Knowledge of the practice of love comes from the science of love (kāmaśāstra), for the subject matter of poetry abounds in the practice of love. //8//
The science of government consists of policy and its opposite.
"From the science of polity (arthaśāstra) [comes] the knowledge of policy (naya), non-policy (apanaya), and their combination.
In this context, "policy" (naya) is the correct application of the sixfold set of measures (ṣāḍguṇya);
its opposite is "non-policy" (apanaya).
For it is not possible to compose a poetic work without first understanding the conduct of both the protagonist and the antagonist. //9//
And from that, there arises the crookedness of what has occurred.
Histories and the like constitute the narrative body of poetry;

its "crookedness" (complexity) arises from the application of the principles of statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*), such as strength and weakness, because that science is rooted in practical proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
In this same manner, the utility of other sciences should also be described according to their respective roles. //10//
Knowledge of the target, diligent application, service to the elders, observation, intuition, and attentiveness constitute miscellaneous [qualities]. (VKal 1.3.11)
In this context, familiarity with poetry consists in the knowledge of its defining characteristics (*lakṣya*).
Familiarity with the works of others means knowledge of the characteristics [of poetry];
for from that, proficiency in the composition of poetry arises. //12//
Exertion is the undertaking of composing poetry.
*Bandhana* means binding;
the composition (*bandha*) of poetry is *kāvyabandha*. In that regard, *udyama* means exertion or application.
For that indeed bestows excellence upon poetic composition. //13//
Service to teachers of poetry and instruction, and attendance upon the elderly.
In the instruction of poetry, the teachers are the instructors; attending upon them is service to the elders. From that, the transmission of the science of poetry occurs. //14//
The laying down of the foot, the lifting up, and the looking.
The placing of the foot is its setting down (nyāsa),
and the lifting is its removal (uddharaṇa);
indeed, it is the observation of these two.
On this point there are two verses:
"As long as the mind wavers between placing and removing [the word],
alas, once stability is established for the word, Sarasvatī herself has been mastered."
That which causes words to abandon their susceptibility to repetition is called "maturity of sound" (śabdapāka) by those expert in the arrangement of words. //15//
The seed of poetry is creative intuition (*pratibhāna*).
The seed of poetry (*kavitva-bīja*) is a certain specific latent impression (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*) brought over from previous births;
without which poetry would not be produced, or if produced, it would become an object of ridicule. //16//
One-pointedness of mind is focused attention.
One-pointedness of mind is the cessation of external objects; it is the focused attention [of the mind]. For when the mind is focused, it perceives objects. //17//
That [is established] by means of place and time. (VK 1.3.18)
That attentiveness arises from both place and time. //18//
Regarding the question of what place and time are, he says here:
"A secluded place. (VKal 1.3.19)
Secluded means devoid of people. //19//
The fourth watch of the night is the time [for this].
A watch of the night (*rātriyāma*) is a *prahara*; it is the fourth part, the fourth period.
By means of that [period], the mind, withdrawn from sense objects, becomes serene and focused. //20//
Having thus demonstrated the components of poetry, he speaks for the sake of understanding the specific types of poetry: "Poetry is both prose and verse. (VKal 1.3.21)
Prose (*gadya*) is mentioned first because it is difficult to compose due to its subject matter being hard to discern;
as they say: "They say that prose is the touchstone for poets. (21)
And in order to show that it is divided into three types, he says:
prose, prose with the scent of verse, and prose consisting mostly of *utkalikā* (rhythmic prose).
He states the characteristics of the *tallakṣaṇa*: "That which possesses the scent of meter (*vṛtta*) like a portion of verse (*padyabhāga*). (VKal 1.3.23)
"Parts of a verse" (padyabhāga) refers to portions of a verse; that which possesses such [parts] is "resembling a meter" (vṛttagandhi).
For example: *pātālatālutalavāsiṣu dānaveṣu*.
Here, indeed, a portion of the meter known as Vasantatilakā is recognized. //23//
The *cūrṇa* [meter] consists of unperforated and graceful feet.

That which consists of words that are not harsh (*anāviddha*), not overly long compounds (*adīrgha-samāsa*), graceful (*lalita*), and not arrogant (*anuddhata*) is called *cūrṇa* (polished prose), characterized by such "graceful and unharsh words. For example:
"For practice indeed brings skill in actions;
for even a drop of water does not create a depression on a stone merely by falling upon it once. (24)
The opposite [of that] consists primarily of agitation (utkalikā).
The opposite is the *āviddhota* (twisted) style, which consists mostly of confused or harsh words; for example:

"In the lion, whose beautiful mane was radiant with the mass of manes drenched by the streams of rut trickling from the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants split open by the fierce blow of claws as hard as the tip of a thunderbolt. (25)
Metre has many varieties.
Indeed, *padya* (verse) is divided by many distinctions, such as *sama*, *ardhasama*, *viṣama*, and so forth. //26//
That is both unbound and bound.
This poetry, consisting of prose and verse, is both uncomposed (anibaddha) and composed (nibaddha).
Since these two types are well known, their definition has not been stated. //27//
The sequential establishment of these two is like a garland and its crest-jewel.
The words "of those two" refer to both the uncomposed and the composed [literary works].
"Success in sequence" (kramasiddhi) means success achieved in a sequential manner.
In the case of success regarding the uncomposed, it is like a garland or an ear-ornament [formed] by means of success regarding the composed.
Just as when a garland has been prepared, the crest-ornament (uttaṃsa) or topknot (śekhara) is thereby established. //28//
Some [arguments] terminate without being connected;
in order to refute that, he says: "That which is unconnected does not shine forth, like a single atom of light. (VKal 1.3.29)
Indeed, poetry that is not structured does not shine or gleam,
just like a single atom of light. Regarding this, there is a verse:
Poems that have not been composed as a unified whole possess no beauty; individual atoms of light do not manifest their brilliance on their own. (29)
Among literary compositions, the *daśarūpaka* (the ten types of drama) is the most excellent.
Among compositions and literary works, the ten forms of drama, such as the *nāṭaka* and others, are the most excellent. //30//
Why is that? It says:
"For that [consciousness] is variegated, like a variegated cloth, because of the completeness of its particulars. (VKal 1.3.31)
For that ten-fold drama is indeed variegated like a painted cloth, because of the completeness of its particular features. //31//
From that, the postulation of other distinctions [arises].
Therefore, the "construction" (kḷpti) or conceptualization of other varieties besides the ten forms of drama means that all of this is merely an elaboration of the ten forms themselves—
namely, the *kathā*, the *ākhyāyikā*, and the *mahākāvya*.
Furthermore, since the description of that [tallness] as a characteristic is not particularly heart-appealing, we have omitted it;
it should be sought elsewhere. //32//
Thus ends the third chapter in the first section, titled "The Body," of the *Śrī Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtra-vṛtti*.
And thus ends this first section, the *Śārīra* (The Body).

**The Second Section: Chapter One** Since the body of poetry has been established, the defects (*doṣas*) must be understood so that those factors which obstruct the beauty of poetry may be abandoned. Therefore, the section entitled "The Examination of Defects" (*Doṣadarśana*) is now commenced.
To explain the nature of the defects (doṣa), he says: "The defects consist in the reversal of the qualities (guṇa). (VKal 2.1.1)
The defects (doṣas) are those whose nature consists of the opposites of the qualities (guṇas) that are about to be described. //1//
Its comprehension occurs through the meaning.
From the definition of the nature of their qualities, the understanding of those defects follows by implication; that is, they are established through implication. //2//
To the question, "For what purpose are these explained separately?", he says: "The detailed exposition is for the sake of ease. (VKal 2.1.3)
The detailed elaboration of the defects is for the sake of ease;
for when the defects have been enumerated and defined by their characteristics, they become easy to understand. //3//
To demonstrate the faults of words, he says: "A defective word is one that is ungrammatical, harsh, vulgar, unintelligible, or meaningless. (VKal 2.1.4)
To explain this in sequence, he says:
"That which is contrary to the traditional knowledge of words is incorrect. (VKal_2.1.5)
A word that contradicts grammar through its conflict with linguistic convention (*śabdasmṛti*) is incorrect (*asādhu*).
For example: *anyakārakavaiyarthyam*.
For in this case, according to the rule *aṣaṣṭhyatṛtīyāsthasyānyasya dugāśīrāśāsthāsthitotsukotikārakarāgaccheṣu*, the substitution of *du* ought to have occurred [for the *n* of *anya*]. //5//
It is painful and discordant with the sacred scriptures.
A word that is discordant with the ear, harsh to the hearing, and painful—even if it is woven into a poetic composition—it causes distress. For example:
*acūcuraccaṇḍi*.
The moon, becoming clear, quickly entered the liquid luster upon his cheeks. //6//
That which is employed merely for the sake of worldly convention is the vulgar.
That word which is employed only in common worldly usage and not in technical treatises is called *grāmya* (vulgar).
For example: "How does she weep so painfully? Why is this sobbing?"
Other things as well, such as the *talla* and *galla*, should be understood in this same way. //7//
That which is employed solely by the treatise is "unrecognized. VKal_2,1.8 //
A word that is employed only in technical treatises and not in common worldly usage is an "unrecognized" (*apratīta*) term. For example:
"What is the use of much speaking? I possess no qualities within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)."
And since valid cognition is invariably concomitant with its qualities, you have no grounds for censure.
In this context, the term "in the world" (*loka*) is not understood as being inseparable from the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). //8//
That which is for the sake of filling [the verse] is meaningless.
An indeclinable word (*avyayapada*) that serves the sole purpose of filling out the meter is meaningless;
by the logic of "the staff and the rice" (*daṇḍāpūpa-nyāya*), any other such word is likewise meaningless. For example:
"But the sun, having drunk up the darkness—which was as dark as a herd of elephants—with its rays, has risen..."
In this case, however, the word "tu" is employed solely for the purpose of filling out the meter;
it is not for the purpose of embellishing the sentence.
Indeed, the purpose of embellishing a sentence is not without meaning.
This is for the purpose of an exception;
however, its function as a poetic embellishment (*vākyālaṅkāra*) is not without purpose.
Just as—indeed, they have not gone here within the range of my vision; for they have truly departed, alas! //9//
Now he states the defects of the word-meaning (padārtha):
"Those that lead to another meaning, those with a hidden meaning, the indecorous, and the obscure. [VKal 2.1.10]
The term "defective word" (*duṣṭaṃ padam*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Furthermore, there is a modification of the grammatical number according to the sense.
The meaning of the sūtra is that words whose meanings are different from what is intended and so forth are defective. //10//
He states the definition of these in sequence: "That which has fallen away from its conventional usage [and] has another meaning. (VKal 2.1.11) [VKal 2.1.12]
"Deviation from conventional usage" means that a word is employed for another meaning by taking up only its etymological sense,
without regard for its conventional usage.
Because of its broad scope, the word "pot" (ghaṭa) and the word "cloth" (paṭa), and so forth, were not mentioned as having other meanings. For example:
"Those who forget their dear associations bring about (āvahanti) various kinds of suffering.
Here, the root *vah* (to carry/bring), which means "to do," is employed in the sense of "to sustain" or "to produce."
The root *smṛ* has the sense of forgetting; [the prefix *pra-*] indicates excellent remembrance. //11//
That which has a conceptualized object is of interpretable meaning.

*Neiyārtha* (interpretable meaning) refers to that which has a constructed meaning because it involves the postulation of a sense not explicitly stated by the words, even if that sense is to be inferred. For example:

"Immediately, the army of monkeys, joined by the son who bears the name of the bird of the line (*paṅktivihaṅgama*), was defeated by the conqueror of owls (*ulūkajit*) with sharp arrows capable of piercing even massive mountains, discharged by the powerful one. [In this verse, the term *paṅktivihaṅgama* is interpreted as referring to Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, who is the leader of the monkey host.]
Here, the bird intended is the *cakravāka* (ruddy sheldrake).
Their names are *cakrāṇi*;
those who bear these names are the "chariots bearing the names of birds."
The word *paṅkti* indicates the number ten.
He whose chariots were ten, bearing the names of birds (*vihaṅgama*), was Daśaratha, known as Paṅktivihaṅgamanāmabhṛt.
By his two sons, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the army of monkeys was conquered.
"By Ulūkajit" means by Indrajit.
Since the word *kauśika* is a designation for both Indra and an owl (*ulūka*), Indra is referred to here as an "owl" because he is denoted by the word *kauśika*.
But if this is so, would it not follow that the usage of names such as "Rathāṅga" (the wheel) [for Aruṇa] would also be untenable?
No; because they possess a conventional, established secondary meaning (nirūḍhalakṣaṇa). //12//
That which employs words whose meanings are not well-known is "obscure" (gūḍhārtha).
When a word has a meaning that is both well-known and unknown in the world, and it is employed in its unknown sense, it is "obscure in meaning" (gūḍhārtha). For example:
"His army, like that of one possessing a thousand cows, was difficult for enemies to withstand because of its great size."
He who has a thousand cows as his eyes is Indra, the possessor of a thousand rays;
thus, the word *go* (cow) being used here to denote "eye" is not well-known among poets. //13//
Inappropriate speech is that which has a different meaning than intended, and indecent speech is that which causes a lack of right mindfulness.
When a word has multiple meanings and one of those meanings is indecent, it is "another meaning that is indecent.
For example— the word *varcas* [has the meanings] of splendor and excrement.
However, that word which, although denoting a refined meaning, causes the recollection of an unrefined meaning by way of a partial similarity, is a cause for the recollection of the unrefined;
for example— the word *kṛkāṭikā*.
They are not concealed, characterized, or restrained.
This is for the purpose of exclusion:
that which is guarded, characterized, and conventional is not vulgar. //15//
He states their characteristics:
"That which is unestablished, improper, and secret [is *apratīta*]. [VKal 2.1.16–17]
A word that has an unknown or vulgar secondary meaning is "obscure-vulgar" (*aprasiddhāsabhya*); that which is thus [used] is "guarded" (*gupta*).
For example, the word *saṃbādha*. For that word is well-known in the sense of "narrowness" (*saṃkaṭa*), [yet it is used here with a different, vulgar sense].
Not for the sake of a secret matter. //16//
That which is endowed with characteristic and unrefined [speech] is defined as *lakṣita*.
That very word, which has another indecent meaning, is defined as one that is connected with an indecent sense through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For example: *janmabhūḥ* ("place of birth").
For that [word], by way of indication, refers to a quality (*guṇa*).
"Not by one's own power. //17//
"Enveloped by the world" means covered.

"Enveloped by the world" (*lokasaṃvīta*) means that which is covered by the world; for example, as in "the womb of a fortunate woman" (*subhagā-bhagonī-upasthāna*), where the intended meaning is the longing of a maiden.
Regarding this, there is a verse: [Verse omitted]
For when one is covered by the world, it is not appropriate to search for faults;
when the Śiva-linga is established, who would conceive of its being indecent? (18)
The threefold nature of the tantras arises from the distinction between those that produce shame, disgust, and inauspicious fear.
That indecorousness (aślīla) is of three kinds, due to the distinction between those that produce shame, disgust, or inauspicious dread.
Some of it produces shame.
For example: *vāk-kāṭava-m-hiraṇyaretāḥ* (the fire whose fuel is speech and wood).
Some [words] produce a sense of disgust;
for example: *kapardakaḥ* (a cowrie shell).
Something may cause apprehension regarding inauspiciousness, as for example: "he is standing. (19)
Defiled [cognition] is that which perceives an object through an intervention.

The cognition of an object is "object-cognition" (*arthapratyaya*). That which arises from something that is separated [from the object] is "separated-object-cognition," which is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). For example:
"Of the beloveds of the daughter of Dakṣa... and so forth.
Drops of water, shimmering with the moonlight, fall tremulously.
The daughters of Dakṣa are the stars;
their beloved is the moon, the beloved of the daughters of Dakṣa;
his favorites are the moonstones.
Regarding the phrase "of those altars": for here, the comprehension of the meaning occurs through an intervention. //20//
Because it is not established elsewhere.
VKal_2,1.21 [k: not in sutra] //
Even when not explicitly stated, that [expression] is not considered "defiled" (kliṣṭa) if it produces an immediate understanding of the intended meaning; for example:
"The state of virtue of the blameless one. //21//
The statement has been explained by the last two [sūtras].
The final two terms are "indecent" (aślīla) and "afflicted" (kliṣṭa).
By these two, speech is explained;
that [speech] as well becomes indecent and afflicted.
An example of the indecorous (*aślīla*) is as follows:
"That is no exaltation by wealth which does not bestow happiness in this life;
for those who have girded their loins for the sake of others, true wealth is that which is meager."
Leaving behind the staircase, which was being tossed by the force of the wind,
he proceeded along the main road while his virtues were being proclaimed by the people.
An example of the defiled [type of beauty]:
Whose mind does not become intensely impassioned upon beholding the beauty of Dhammillā’s braided hair— she who has eyes like those of a young deer— due to its unprecedented arrangement?
The intended meaning is that, having recognized these defects of words and word-meanings, the poet should abandon them. //22//
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Classification of Defects of Words and Word-Meanings," in the second section, "The Observation of Defects," of the *Śrī Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtra-vṛtti*.
In the second section, the second chapter begins.
Having explained the defects of words and word-meanings, the author now speaks in order to demonstrate the defects of sentences: [Text follows...]
Sentences that have broken meters, misplaced pauses, or faulty euphonic combinations.
The connection with wicked policy. //1//
He explains them in sequence:
"That which has deviated from its own characteristic is one whose function is divided. (VKal 2.2.2)
A sentence in which the meter has deviated from its own characteristic is called *svalakṣaṇacyuta* (deviation from its own characteristic) or *bhinnavṛtta* (broken meter). For example:
"O, do you see her resting upon the palace, wearing a garland of dense flowers?"
In the even feet of the Vaitālīya meter, the immediate succession of six short syllables is prohibited;
since that has been committed here, there is a violation of the metrical rule (bhinnavṛttatva). //2//
That which lacks heroic sentiment is "devoid of heroism" (virasa), and that which lacks the proper pause is "fallen from the caesura" (yatibhraṣṭa).
That which has a discordant pause—meaning a pause that is unpleasant to the ear—is *virasavirāma*, or "discordant pause," and it constitutes a lapse in caesura (*yatibhraṣṭa*). //3//
In the division of the parts of those roots and names, this generally occurs when vowel-sandhi has been applied.
That [fault] occurs when there is a division of the verbal root portion (*dhātubhāga*) and a division of the nominal portion (*nāmabhāga*), having occurred primarily—
that is, for the most part— due to vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*).
As an example of the division of the verbal root portion in *mandākrāntā* meter:

The spreading perspiration upon the surface of the cheeks of these fawn-eyed women, hanging like a garland of flowers around their necks, shines forth according to the distinction of their names, as in the Śikhariṇī meter.
As in the *mandākrāntā* meter:
"The staff-like arm of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, tawny like the fire of a wheel, is difficult to behold.
Because of the inclusion of the words *dhātu*, *nāma*, *bhāga*, and *pada*, there is no violation of the caesura (*yatibhraṣṭatva*) even when there is a division exceeding that [prescribed] portion.
As in the *mandākrāntā* meter:
"The awakening of beautiful women brings forth a fresh splendor.
As in the *śikhariṇī* meter:
At the edges of their dark-complexioned faces, they were sleepless due to the whistling sounds from the corners of their lips;
for according to the rule "there is no fault in a division caused by *svarasandhi*," there is no defect in a division produced by *svarasandhi*. For example:
"The glances of the beautiful women were somewhat languid with emotion and straightforward. (4)
The fault of caesura is not distinct from the fault of meter, because meter consists essentially of caesura.
The fault of *yati* need not be mentioned separately from the fault of *vṛtta*, because *vṛtta* consists essentially of *yati*. //5//

Since a metrical foot (*vṛtta*) is defined by its caesura (*yati*), a violation of the caesura is already included within the category of "irregular meter" (*bhinnavṛtta*); therefore, it should not be mentioned separately.
To this he replies: "No, because their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinct. (VKal 2.2.6)
This is not a fault, because the definition and the defined are distinct; for the definition of *vṛtta* is one thing, while that of *yati* is another.
*Vṛtta* consists of the regulation of heavy and light syllables.
And the pause (yati) consists of a cessation [of the recitation]. //6//
A hiatus between words that is discordant due to their irregular form is *visaṃdhi*.
The junction of words (*pada*) is "word-junction" (*padasandhi*). That [junction] consists either of the combination of vowels (*svarasamavāya*) or of mere proximity (*pratyāsattimātra*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which there is such a multiform [junction]. //7//
The irregularity of word-junction consists of disjunction, vulgarity, and harshness.
Separation, harshness through division— separation is as follows:
by this wind from the clouds, in this mountain grove...
This series of graceful charms binds these eyes as if they were lotuses;
faces adorned with dangling locks of hair shine brightly.
As for vulgarity (*aślīlatva*): [example follows].
This dance, performed by the semblance of teachers, was a purgative;
the city shone with great trees of learning that were mostly jackfruit-bearing,
eager for verbal debate even without oaths or formal pledges.
An example of difficulty (*kaṣṭatva*) is as follows:
"Those trees, heavy with their fullness and containing the emergence of flower-clusters, shone forth. (8)

Having thus stated the defects of the sentence, he speaks in order to demonstrate the defects of the sentence-meaning: "The senseless, the single-meaninged, the doubtful, the illogical, the misplaced, and those contrary to worldly convention and to science. (VKal 2.2.9)
The connection is that [these] sentences are defective. //9//
To explain them in order, he says:
"That whose preceding and succeeding meanings are contradictory is 'meaningless' (vyartha). (VKal_2.2.10)
A sentence whose prior and subsequent meanings are contradictory is one with "contradictory prior and subsequent meanings" (*vyāhatapūrvottarārtha*), and such a sentence is useless. For example:
"Even now my mind remembers the languid gestures of that charming girl, which were so skillful in love."
"How can the actions of a simple girl be clever in matters of love?
And if they are so, how can she be simple?
Here, because of the contradiction between the preceding and following meanings, the statement is futile. //10//
A word whose meaning has already been stated is synonymous with one that has a single meaning.
A "single-meaning" (ekārtha) [compound] is one in which the words have already expressed their meanings; for example:
"The sidelong glance of the fair-browed woman spreads thought, delusion, and passion, O dear one."
Anaṅga is the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Because it consists of anxiety and delusion, the words "anxiety" (cintā) and "delusion" (moha) are employed, which convey the aforementioned meaning.
Since the words have a single unified sense, it is said that the sentence possesses a single unified meaning. //11//
No; if there is a distinction [in meaning], that which has the same referent is not defective.
It is not defective if it has already been understood, provided that a further distinction is to be established. (12)
To demonstrate that distinction, he says: "The word 'bow' [is used] for both the bow and its string in order to convey the state of being strung. (VKal 2.2.13)

In the expression "the sound of the bowstring" (*dhanurjyādhvani*), although the meaning has already been conveyed by the word *jyā* (bowstring), the mention of the word *dhanus* (bow) is employed for the purpose of making the act of mounting known— that is,
for the sake of making the mounting known.
For indeed, without the mention of the word "bow," it is not possible to understand that the string fixed upon a bow is called "bow-string" (dhanurjyā), as in the example:
"Your arm, marked by the calluses of the bow-string, throbbed. (13)
The mention of "ear" and so forth in the expressions "ear-ornament," "ear-ring," and "head-garland" occurs because of their proximity [to those parts].

In expressions such as *karṇāvataṃsa* ("ear-ornament"), the mention of "ears" (*karṇa*) and so forth—even though their meaning is already conveyed by words like "ornament" (*avataṃsa*)—is for the purpose of conveying their proximity; this is the connection [of the argument].
For indeed, without the mention of the word "ear" and so forth, it would not be possible to convey that the ornaments are situated upon the ears. As it is said:
"During the playful swings of the graceful women, the ear-ornaments partake in the trembling."
Moving playfully, they fell upon his ear-ornaments; adorned with crests, they arrived swiftly, resonant with the humming of bees. //14//
In the compound word *muktāhāra*, the term *muktā* [is used] because of its purity.

In the compound "muktāhāra," the word *muktā* (pearl) is employed even though its meaning is already conveyed by the word *hāra* (necklace); this is for the purpose of conveying purity—this is the connection. A necklace consisting of pure pearls, unmixed with other gems, is a *muktāhāra*. For example: [as in the following verse].
Through the playful movements of embracing her lord of life,
her two breasts seem to laugh with their shimmering pearl necklace.
In the compound "flower-garland" (*puṣpamālā*), the word "flower" (*puṣpa*) [expresses] excellence.
In the term *puṣpamālā* (flower-garland), the word *puṣpa* (flower) is employed even though its meaning is already conveyed by the word *mālā* (garland) alone;
this is for the purpose of conveying excellence (*utkarṣa*).
For example, it is like saying "a garland of flowers" (*puṣpamālā*) to indicate a garland made of superior flowers.
"Whom would that maiden not entice, being for the most part like a garland of flowers?
Indeed, the word 'mālā' is seen elsewhere as well;
for example, *ratnamālā* (a string of jewels)."
"It is merely sound": true;
that is, for the time being, it is the application of a metaphorical designation.
For the word *mālā*, when used without an accompanying qualifier, denotes specifically a particular arrangement of flowers. //16//
In the expression "young elephant" (*karikalabha*), the word "elephant" (*kari*) [denotes the young elephant] by way of identity (*tādrūpya*).

In the compound *karikalabha* (young elephant), the word *kari* (elephant) is employed even though its meaning is already conveyed by *kalabha* (calf); this is for the purpose of conveying its specific nature (*tādrūpya*).
An "elephant" (*karī*) is a mature tusker; a calf that possesses that same nature is a "young elephant" (*karikalabha*). For example: [as in the following verse].
O young elephant, abandon your bond of affection for the female elephant. //17//
And [the same applies] to the qualifier.
The employment of a word whose meaning has already been stated for the purpose of conveying a specific distinction [is *viśeṣaṇa*]. For example:
"He spoke sweet words, characterized by clear syllables. (18)
This [is the case] regarding those who have been engaged. // VKal_2.2.19 //
This has been stated regarding those [words] that are employed,
not regarding those that are not employed; for it is not the case, as for example—
"O you with earrings on your ears!
Thus [it is said], and likewise: "O you with a girdle upon your hips!"
Or as in the case of "a young elephant" (*karikalabha*),
so too is there the expression "a young camel" (*uṣṭrakalabha*).
On this point, there is a verse:

In expressions such as *karṇāvataṃsa* ("ear-ornament"), the word *karṇa* ("ear") is employed for the sake of indicating proximity and so forth, even though [the ear] is already present [as part of the compound]. This is the justification for its use. //19//
That which creates doubt is "doubtful. (VKal 2.20)
A statement that creates doubt because it mentions either common attributes or specific attributes is "doubt-creating" (*saṃśayakṛt*) or "ambiguous" (*sandigdha*). For example:
"That great-souled one, by the power of fortune, has attained a high position. [The ambiguity is:
"Has he attained a high position by the power of fortune? [or by some other cause?]
"Or rather, has he fallen into great calamity due to the power of misfortune?"—this is a statement that creates doubt when there is an absence of context and other such factors. //20//
It is employed for the purpose of objects conceptualized as being like illusions and so forth.

That in which an object is imagined through illusion (māyā) and so forth is "that in which an object is imagined through illusion and so forth" (māyādikalpitārtha); this term is not employed [as a compound].
Herein is a brief illustration. //21//
That which lacks the proper sequence is called *apakrama*.

The sequence (*krama*) of those things that have been mentioned and those that have not been mentioned is "connection" (*sambandha*). That meaning which is devoid of this is "meaning lacking sequence," i.e., "out-of-order" (*apakrama*). For example:
"Fame and splendor are equal to the sun and the moon."
In this case, his fame is equal to that of the moon,
and his majesty is equal to that of the sun;
the lack of proper order arises because the word for "sun" (sūrya) has been placed first.
Alternatively, *krama* (proper order) is the indication of the principal matter.
That in which a matter is devoid of that [order] is *apakrama* (disordered). For example:
"Then give him a horse and an elephant languid with rut. (22)
Those whose meanings contradict place, time, and intrinsic nature are contrary to the world.
Sentences whose meanings are contradicted by place, time, or inherent nature are "sentences with meanings contradictory to place, time, and inherent nature," which are contrary to worldly convention.
The contradiction with worldly convention in these sentences occurs by way of their meaning.
An example of what is contradictory to place is as follows:
In the Sauvīra country there is a famous city named Madhurā,
whose surrounding lands abound in walnuts and coconuts.
An example of what is contrary to the season (*kālaviruddha*) is:
"In the spring, the forest shone, blooming with *kadamba* flowers.
An example of what is contrary to nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*) is:
And in the clusters of *saptacchada* blossoms, resonant with the humming of intoxicated bees, the beauty of autumn’s bliss seems to be dancing;
for while it is the nature of the *saptacchada* tree to produce clusters (*stavaka*), not flower-stalks (*mañjarī*), this [description] is contrary to its natural state. Likewise—
The bee pressed upon the interior of the flower bud so intensely that it caused a profusion of honey to rain down, filling the hoofprint of a cow.
Such an abundance of nectar from every single bud is contrary to its very nature. //23//
Those meanings which contradict the arts and the treatises on the four aims of human life are contrary to knowledge. 2.24.
Sentences whose meanings are contradicted by the arts (kalā) and the treatises on the four aims of life (caturvarga-śāstra) are those with meanings contrary to the sciences;
thus, the contradiction of sentences occurs through their meaning.
An example of that which is contrary to the arts (kalā-śāstra) is as follows:
"Friend, this letter was written by Kāliṅga; for those skilled in epistolary art, the tip of the thorn [the seal] must not be fallen-off.
It is the tradition of those who know letters that a Kāliṅga letter has a fallen-off tip of the thorn.
Because it contradicts that, it is contrary to the science of arts (kalāśāstra)."
In this manner, contradictions should also be inferred regarding other arts (*kalā*).
However, those that contradict the treatises on the four aims of life (*caturvarga*) are illustrated as follows:
"The conquest of the earth by kings has as its sole fruit the complete enjoyment of sensual pleasures."
The traditional teaching (āgama) states that the fruit of dharma is the fruit of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, or for kings, the conquest of the earth;
therefore, because it contradicts that, this statement has a meaning opposed to the Dharmaśāstras. [For it asks: "Are enemies not conquered by pride? What is the use of the glory of policy?"
In the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), it is established that the conduct of kings is rooted in policy;
therefore, a statement that contradicts this is said to be contrary to the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*).
I remember her face, its upper lip sanctified by the marks of his teeth, languid with the exhaustion of love-making.
"Excluding the upper lip, the interior of the mouth, and the corners of the eyes, these are the places for kissing, scratching, and biting"—
thus it is established in the *Kāmaśāstra*.
Because it contradicts that, the statement is one whose meaning is contrary to the *Kāmaśāstra*.
Liberation comes from devotion to the deity, not from the possession of knowledge of reality;
for this point is established in the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*), and [the aforementioned views] are contrary to that meaning.
These defects of sentence and sentence-meaning must be known so as to be abandoned.

However, those other subtle defects of word and meaning are observed in the analysis of the poetic qualities (*guṇa*), while the defects of simile are treated in the investigation of simile (*upamā*). //24//
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Classification of Defects of Sentence and Sentence-Meaning," in the second section, "The Examination of Defects," of the *Śrī Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti*. 2.2.
And thus concludes the second section (*adhikaraṇa*), the "Observation of Faults" (*doṣadarśana*).
The first chapter of the third section begins.
Since faults are of the nature of the opposites of those [qualities], this section, the "Discernment of Qualities" (*guṇavivecana*), is commenced in order to investigate those qualities.

In this regard, it is the established view of those learned in poetry that qualities such as vigor (*ojas*) and clarity (*prasāda*) are *guṇas* (qualities), whereas figures such as parallelism (*yamaka*) and simile (*upamā*) are *alaṅkāras* (ornaments).
To the question of what constitutes the basis for their distinction, he says: "The *guṇas* are those properties that produce the beauty of poetry. (VKal 3.1.1)
Indeed, those properties of word and meaning which produce the beauty of poetry are the *guṇas* (excellences); and these are *ojas* (vigour) and *prasāda* (clarity),
not *yamaka* (paronomasia), *upamā* (simile), and so forth.
Because, according to Kauṇḍinya, these [qualities] do not produce the beauty of poetry;
however, *ojas*, *prasāda*, and the others possess the quality of producing the beauty of poetry when they exist alone. //1//
The causes of its excellence are the poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra).

The "excess" (*atiśaya*) of that poetic beauty is "its excess"; the causes of that [excess] are the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), such as *yamaka*, *upamā*, and so forth. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction.
On this point there are two verses:

Just as the beauty of a young woman, even when pure in its qualities, is exceedingly pleasing, so too does poetry taste most sweet when it possesses pure qualities and is graced with the application of various ornaments through continuous and well-executed poetic conceits.
If speech falls away from virtues, like the body of a woman devoid of youth, then even ornaments that are beloved by people will inevitably fall into a state of misfortune. //2//
The former are eternal.
The primary qualities (guṇas) are eternal, because without them the splendor of poetry would be impossible. //3//
Having thus shown the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), he speaks for the purpose of defining the qualities of sound (*śabdaguṇa*):

"Force (*ojas*), clarity (*prasāda*), cohesion (*śleṣa*), evenness (*samatā*), concentration (*samādhi*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), softness (*saukumārya*), loftiness (*audāratā*), explicitness of meaning (*arthavyakti*), and beauty (*kānti*) are the qualities of composition (*bandhaguṇa*). (VKal 3.1.4)
Bandha is the arrangement of words;
its qualities (guṇas) are the qualities of composition (bandhaguṇas), such as *ojas* and so forth. //4//
To demonstrate these in sequence, he says:
"Ojas is the state of firm binding. (VKal 3.1.5)
Just as they cause the flower clusters, from which the nectar has been shaken loose, to dance;
but not again—
They cause the flower-clusters, from which streams of honey flow, to sway. //5//
Relaxation is clarity.
The relaxation of the bodily bonds is their loosening, which is tranquility. //6//
But surely this is a defect consisting in the opposite of *ojas*; so how can it be a quality? To this he says:
"It is a quality because of their coalescence. (VKal 3.1.7)
The quality is clarity (prasāda), because it coexists with vigor (ojas). //7//
It is not pure.
But that which is pure is indeed a fault. //8//
Now, one might ask: how can there be a coalescence (*saṃplava*) of the two contradictory qualities, *ojas* and *prasāda*? To this, he says:
"But that [coalescence] is established by experience. (VKal 3.1.9) [cf. VKal 3.1.8]
But that convergence is established by experience,
like the specific qualities of gems and such for those who know them.
On this point, there is a verse:
Just as the commingling of pleasure and pain is established through direct experience in those things worthy of compassionate regard, so too is it established for vitality and clarity. //9//
And [it concerns] equality and superiority.
Equanimity and excellence belong only to *ojas* and *prasāda*. Equanimity is, for example:
"Then he, with his mind withdrawn from sense objects, according to the prescribed rule for his son..."
Having bestowed the white sunshade—the emblem of sovereignty—upon the youth (Raghu).
In some instances, [the quality] *ojas* is superior due to *prasāda* (clarity), as for example:
"The sky bears a resemblance to the fruit of the *bhallātaka* tree..."
In some cases, there is an excellence of *ojas* (vigorous energy) and *prasāda* (transparency), as for example:
Neither a bed of flowers, nor the rays of the moon, nor sandalwood paste applied to every limb, nor jeweled pillars [could bring relief]. //10//
Smoothness is *śleṣa* (cohesion).
Smoothness (*masṛṇatvam*) is that quality in which many words appear as one. For example:
"In the northern direction there exists the king of mountains named Himālaya, whose nature is divine. But not, for instance: [an example of lack of smoothness].
The Sūtra is in the Brahma-region of the chest;
there are the charming songs of the Bhramarīs,
and the sky is filled with lightning.
In this way, however, there is a pun: "The Vedic thread upon the chest,
and the humming songs of the female bees."
"The sky is matted with lightning. //11//
The non-confusion of the path is equanimity.

The non-differentiation of the path (*mārgābheda*) is its uniformity (*samatā*); the meaning is that one does not abandon the very path by which one has begun. The examples previously mentioned apply both to the verse (*śloka*) and to the composition (*prabandha*).
The opposite case is as follows:
"Be gracious, O fierce one! Abandon your anger immediately; this person stands before you with palms joined in reverence."
For what reason do you remain thus, with your playful grace lost and your pair of full breasts trembling? // 12 //
Samādhi is the sequence of ascent and descent.
The sequence of ascent and descent is the "sequence of ascent and descent"; this is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that constitutes the resolution.
It is the resolution when there is descent following ascent, or ascent following descent.
In that regard, descent preceded by ascent is as follows:
"Men fallen from virtue sink like trees in calamity.
The sequence of ascent and the sequence of descent together constitute the sequence of ascent and descent (*ārohāvarohakrama*).
Some say there is both ascent and descent in sequence, as follows:
"The settling of the celestial river upon the paths of the snowy mountains is victorious. (13)
They are not distinct, because *ojas* and *prasāda* constitute the nature of the ascending and descending [movements].

Concentration (*samādhi*) is not a distinct quality, because the ascending (*āroha*) and descending (*avaroha*) movements consist respectively of the qualities of vigor (*ojas*) and clarity (*prasāda*); that is, the ascent is of the nature of vigor, and the descent is of the nature of clarity. //14//
No, because they are not conjoined.
As for what was stated— that *āroha* (ascending) and *avaroha* (descending) consist of *ojas* (vigor) and *prasāda* (lucidity)— that is not so,
because they are intermingled (*sampṛktatvāt*).
Indeed, when *ojas* and *prasāda* are combined, they flow together like two converging streams of rivers. //15//
And because [the reason] is inconclusive.
And this is not an absolute rule—that there must be an ascent in *ojas* and a descent in *prasāda*. (16)
If it is accepted that those two are the intense state of *ojas* and *prasāda*.

If you think that there is an ascent and descent within a certain portion of the *ojas* and *prasāda* when they reach an intense state— that intense state being what is called ascent and descent— then [we respond as follows].
Acceptance is not disagreement. //17//
Because those two depend upon a specific distinction.
That distinction consists of the nature of other qualities. //18//
Concentration is said to be the cause for ascending and descending.
The term "samādhi" should be explained through figurative usage as the sequence of ascending and descending. //19//
Or rather, it is for the purpose of establishing the sequence.
Regarding "separation" (*pṛthakkaraṇa*):
we shall explain in the [sūtra] *na pāṭhadharmāḥ sarvatrādṛṣṭeḥ* (3.1.28) that the status of being a property of recitation (*pāṭhadharmatva*) is also not possible. //20//
Sweetness (*mādhurya*) consists in the distinctness of words.
The quality of having separate words (*pṛthakpadatva*) within a compound is what constitutes sweetness (*mādhurya*). That which possesses separate words is "separate-worded" (*pṛthakpada*);
the state of being such is "the quality of having separate words.
And this [definition] is intended to exclude excessive length of compounds.
Tenderness is the state of being free from coarseness.
That which constitutes the non-rigidity, the absence of harshness,
and the delicacy of a composition has been illustrated by the examples previously mentioned.
The opposite, however, is as follows:

The cause is non-dual, yet the conviction that the beloved person before me is a mere likeness [of her] results in both the sprinkling of nectar and the burning of fire; even the fruit in my heart is contradictory. //22//
Vikaṭatva (the state of being formidable) is udāratā (magnificence).

The "awkwardness" (*vikaṭatva*) of the construction is what constitutes its "loftiness" (*udāratā*). When this exists, there arises in the minds of people the impression that the words are as if dancing; that is "awkwardness.
The meaning is: a state of playful movement. For example: [Example omitted per instructions]
There, the anklets of the dancing girls, fixed upon their own feet, produced a wonderful and melodious *jhaṇiti* sound;
yet it was not [the case that]—[rather], the anklets clinging to the lotus-feet of the dancing girls produced a sweet and wonderful resonance there. //23//
The state of being the cause for the manifestation of meaning is "manifestation of meaning" (*arthavyakti*).
That which serves as the cause for the immediate comprehension of meaning is the quality known as *arhavyakti* (manifestation of the worthy); this is the previously mentioned example.
However, counter-examples are both numerous and easily found. //24//
Brilliance is luster.
The brilliance of the composition is what is called "beauty" (*kānti*);
in its absence, it is said to have the "appearance of antiquity. For example:
*kuraṅgīnetrālīstavakitavanālīparisaraḥ* (The vicinity of the forest rows, thick with rows of deer-eyed women...)
The opposite, however, is more frequent and easier;
and there are verses on this point:
"The masters of poetry declare that firmness of word-arrangement is *ojas* (vigorousness)."
Words presided over by this [power] are for the most part an elixir for the ear.
They declare that clarity (*prasāda*) consists of a mixture of looseness and vigor;
without this, the path of poetry does not truly please.
Where even a multitude of words function as if they were a single word, with no perceptible junctures between them, that is *śleṣa*, the supreme literary quality.
The adoption of a single path in every quarter-verse and in every stanza—
being difficult to compose and difficult to discern— is considered the quality of *samatā* (evenness).
For when ascetics ascend and descend in due order, that quality is called *samādhi*; by it, Sarasvatī was purified.
The wise have declared that sweetness (*mādhurya*) consists in the separation of words within a verse-division (*bandha*).
For by this means, the final syllables of the words flow like streams of honey;
in the same way, speech too, when woven with all the poetic excellences (*guṇa*), is sweet to the wise.
The absence of harshness in composition is declared to be "suavity" (*saukumārya*);
by its absence, words become coarse and thus unfit for hearing.
For they say that the "monstrosity" of a composition refers to its grandeur;
yet by this [grandeur], the sequences of words do not attain variety, being rendered empty.
Where the manifestation of meaning occurs as if speech follows after the object and as if it precedes the object,
that quality is known as *arthavyakti* (manifestation of meaning), because it serves as the cause for the clarity of the sense.
Those expert in the qualities of poetry say that brilliance is the quality known as *kānti* (loveliness). Without it, a poet's speech becomes barren, like an ancient painting. //25//
They are not non-existent, because they are experienced as being existent.
Indeed, these qualities are not non-existent, because they are perceptible. //26//
He says that even though they are cognizable by those who know that [reality],
they would not be deluded—
because they are unwavering. (VKal 3.1.27) [VKal 3.1.26]
The qualities are not erroneous, because the activity directed toward them is unshakable. //27//
They do not have the nature of being recited,
because they are not observed everywhere.
These qualities are not properties of the recitation,
because they are not observed everywhere.
If they were properties of the recitation, then, being independent of specific distinctions, they would be observed everywhere.
Furthermore, they are not observed everywhere;
since particularities are qualities in relation to their substrata, there is indeed an admission of qualities. //28//
Thus ends the first chapter of the third section, titled "Discernment of Qualities," in the Vṛtti on the Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra composed by Vāmana.

[Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Differentiation of Qualities and Figures of Speech" and "The Differentiation of the Qualities of Sound," in the third section, "The Investigation of Qualities," of the *Śrī Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtra-vṛtti*.
Now begins the second chapter of the third section.
Now, for the purpose of discerning the qualities of meaning, he says:
"Those very same things are the qualities of meaning. (VKal 3.2.1)
These very qualities, beginning with *ojas* (vigor), are the qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇa*). //1//
The maturity of meaning is *ojas*.
The maturity (*prauḍhi*) or developed state of the meaning—that which is to be expressed—is *ojas*.
It consists of expressing a sentence-meaning within the meaning of a word, or expressing a word-meaning within the meaning of a sentence;
it also includes maturity through expansion (*vyāsa*) and contraction (*samāsa*), as well as the possession of intentional significance (*sābhiprāyatva*).
Regarding the use of a sentence to express a single word-meaning, as in (Raghuvaṃśa 2.75):
"Then, like the sky [receiving] the light arising from the eyes of Atri...
Here, in place of the word "moon," the sentence "the light arising from the eyes of Atri" has been employed.
And by "sentence" (vākya), a collection of words is intended. In this manner, other cases should also be understood. For example:
"First a pale shadow, followed by a place marked by a brownish hue..."
Then, its body colored by contact with the red quality due to the swelling of ripeness,
the jujube fruit, when beginning to slowly dry in the forest, assumes a state of saplessness, made uneven by its own protruding ridges.
And there is no such over-extension [of the definition],
because the general definition of a quality (*guṇa*) as that which "produces the beauty of poetry" remains established.
The denotation of words within the meaning of a sentence is as follows: for instance,
when it ought to be said that "this woman is not divine, but rather human," one says, "she blinks."
The expansion and contraction of this sentence-meaning are as follows. The expansion is: "This manifold form is the intermingling of pleasure and pain."
Whether it be happiness or suffering, it does not simply cease; rather, from that very state, happiness or suffering arises once again.
Furthermore, beyond that, some form of happiness or suffering arises, yet beyond even that, there is no more suffering.
And it is not happiness.
An example of a compound is as follows (Kumārasambhava 6.94):
"This very son of Candragupta, the youth Candraprakāśa,
has now become by good fortune a king who is the refuge of the wise, his efforts having achieved their purpose."

Furthermore, in the phrase "the refuge of those of perfected intellect," the word *subandhum* possesses intentional meaning (*sābhiprāyatvam*) because it is directed toward the proposal of [Subandhu's] role as minister.
By this, the intentional meaning of the word *sukeśyāḥ* in the verse "In the mass of hair of the fair-haired woman, loosened by passion... is also explained. //2//
Clarity regarding the meaning is lucidity.
Lucidity (*prasāda*) is the clarity of meaning, consisting in the employment of only what is necessary for the purpose. For example:
"Every girl is endowed with the onset of beauty and youth"—but the opposite is as follows: [text missing].
"Let my hand rest upon this girdle-line of pure gems"—here, because the hips are already indicated by the phrase "girdle-line" itself, the qualifier is redundant. //3//
The occurrence [of these] is *śleṣa* (punning condensation). // VKal_3.2.4 //
The application of propriety characterized by gradualness, artfulness, and lack of vulgarity is *ghaṭanā*;
that is *śleṣa* (coalescence).
As in (Amaruśataka 16):
Seeing his two beloveds seated together on a single seat, he approached them from behind with respect;
under the pretext of playfully binding the eyes of one of them,
he slightly turned his neck, his hair standing on end as his heart overflowed with love.
A rogue kisses another woman whose cheeks glisten with a suppressed smile.
An extensive elaboration of this [topic] is seen in the literary compositions written by Śūdraka and others. //4//
Absence of inequality is equanimity.
Non-disparity is the absence of a break in sequence; it is uniformity.
In some cases, even the sequence is broken, as for example:
"The *kunda* flowers have shed their blossoms; the trees are sluggish in the production of new flowers."
These Malaya breezes are blowing, shattering the fortitude of those separated from their lovers;
yet the rays of the sun cut through the cool luster [of the breeze] without assuming that harshness which brings on exhaustion.
In this second quarter-verse, which is intent upon establishing the transition between seasons, there is a change in the sequence [of words], because the Malaya breezes are its unique characteristic.
Thus, the second quarter-verse should be read as follows:
And these cuckoos do not scatter their songs in the mind;
thus [it is said]. //5//
Or, "ease" means the absence of unevenness.
VKal 3.2.6 [k: not in sutra] //
It is understood with ease; that is to say, it is known.
As in (Kumārasambhava 1.1): "There exists in the northern direction a divine being... and so forth.
Or for example:
"Who is this woman with a veil, whose bodily beauty is not clearly visible,
standing in the midst of ascetics like a fresh sprout among pale leaves?"
A counter-example is easily found. //6//
The vision of the object is meditative concentration.
The seeing of an object is "vision" (dṛṣṭi).
It is "concentration" (samādhi) because it is the cause of concentration; for it is a concentrated mind that perceives objects. (1-3-17v)
This has been stated previously. //7//
Meaning is of two kinds:
that which is not born from a source, or that which is born from the shadow of another.
The object whose perception constitutes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is of two kinds: either without origin (*ayoni*) or having another as its source (*anyacchāyāyoni*).
"Without origin" means causeless;
the meaning is that its sole cause is attentive focus (*avadhāna*).
The shadow of another poem (*anyacchāyā*) refers to that which is either its reflection or originates from it. For example:
"Do not fear, O Moon; Rāhu is not in my *śīdhu* wine.
Rohiṇī dwells in the sky; why do you tremble, O coward?"
It is no wonder that the minds of men generally waver during their first encounters with clever women.
The meaning of the first verse is "without a womb" (ayoni), and that of the second is "having a shadow as its womb" (chāyāyoni). //8//
The object is both manifest and subtle.
That object whose perception is called "concentration" (samādhi) is twofold: manifest and subtle.
The manifest has already been clearly explained. //9//
In order to explain the subtle [state], he says: "The subtle is that which is to be cultivated and that which is to be perfumed. (VKal 3.2.10) [cf. VKal 3.2.9]
The subtle [object] is of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) and that which is to be perfumed (*vāsanīya*). That which is accessible through rapid discernment is "to be cultivated."
It is to be cultivated as that which is accessible through the excellence of one-pointedness;
it is to be meditated upon as follows: "The luster of the teeth, mutually blended and thick."

In the pleasure-chamber, during their incessant amorous dalliances, the pair of Cakravāka birds remains present at every moment, their eyes rolling with joy and their pupils half-closed in intense passion.
The manner of being allured is as follows:
Having stood with her hips turned away in feigned modesty, yet with her breasts turned toward me, she looked at me while holding a pearl necklace in her right hand. (10)
Sweetness (*mādhurya*) is the variety of expression.
The variety of expression that exists is what constitutes sweetness (*mādhurya*). For example:
"Nectar is full of flavor; who has any doubt? Even honey is not otherwise."
Even the mango fruit is exceedingly sweet and possesses a clear, pleasant flavor;
yet let a person who is impartial and knowledgeable in other tastes declare, even once, if there is anything else here that is sweeter than the lip of a beloved. (11)
Absence of harshness is gentleness.
In the context of human goals, gentleness is called delicacy;
as they say, "he is dead," meaning "only his fame remains."
"Alone, with the deity as his companion," he says;
"Go, accomplish [the goal]," he says. //12//
The state of being non-vulgar is nobility (*audārya*).
Elegance (*audārya*) consists in the absence of vulgarity when there is the risk of vulgarity; for example:
"You possess such beauty, and he is well-acquainted with loveliness; you two alone, O youth and maiden, reach the very pinnacle of all arts."
O fortunate one, by good fortune, that pair corresponds with your opinion;
if the remainder from this were to be conquered by the multiplier, then [the result] would be won here.
But the contrary was true—having said, "This person nearby sleeps; I shall sleep as long as he does. What is lost to you? she gently took my hand at the waist with her own hand and held it fast. (13)
The manifestation of the object is the clarity of the intrinsic nature of the thing.

The clarity of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things and entities is what constitutes the manifestation of meaning (*arthavyakti*). For example: Upon its back, marked with rows of scales as red as lac against the background of shell-like whiteness, the lotus of the pond—its outer petals tawny and green like *gorocanā* pigment—exhales its fragrance in the water.
Or as it is said:
"First, its tip was covered with fresh filaments; then it stood with broad stamens and very sparse inner petals, slightly closed together."
Thereafter, as the outer petals began the process of budding, they performed only a slight turning, while the old lotuses underwent great distress. //14//
Lustre is the state of having radiant flavor.

*Dīptarasa* refers to that in which the sentiments (*rasas*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, are radiant; the state of being such is *dīptarasatva*, which is brilliance (*kānti*). For example:
"The beloved was sent away at evening by his mistress after she had made him prostrate at her feet with oaths."
Before he had even gone two or three steps from the residential quarters with his mind distracted,
she instead ran forward, clasping his neck and hips with her joined palms, and offered her salutation— oh, how strange is the course of love!
In this same manner, examples should be cited for the other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) as well.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The maturity of poetry (*kāvyapāka*) is said to consist in the clarity and completeness of its qualities (*guṇa*)."
And this [state] is compared to the ripening of a mango.

That poetry which consists essentially of grammatical inflections and verbal suffixes, yet possesses the qualities of a flawed subject matter, would be like the taste of a bitter gourd; therefore, people loathe it.
That speech which lacks a referent for its tenfold qualities is meaningless; such statements as "ten pomegranates" and so forth are words that cannot withstand critical examination.
Thus ends the second chapter in the third section, the Examination of Qualities (*guṇavivecana*), within the *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* composed by the illustrious and eminent scholar Vāmana.
And with this, the third section, the Examination of Qualities, is completed.
Now begins the first chapter of the fourth section.

The beauty of poetry is brought about by the literary excellences (*guṇas*); the ornaments (*alaṅkāras*) are the causes for its intensification. For the purpose of defining these, the section on ornaments (*ālaṅkārika-adhikaraṇa*) is commenced.
Among those, there are verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*).

Therein, he speaks in order to demonstrate the two verbal ornaments, *yamaka* (chiasmus) and *anuprāsa* (alliteration): "Yamaka is the repetition of a word or a syllable with multiple meanings, when its position is fixed. (VKal 4.1.1)

A word has multiple meanings, and a single meaning may belong to one or many words; likewise, *yamaka* (rhyme) occurs when there is no repetition of syllables while the position [of the words] is fixed.
"Positional fixity" means the pervasion of multiple quarters (*pāda*)—either in their entirety or in part—by itself or by its own kind.

As for those instances of *yamaka* seen that occur within a portion of a single quarter, the positional fixity is established only in relation to the placement of *yamaka* found in other verses. //1//
In order to explain the [concept of] "place" (sthāna), he says: "The places are the initial, middle, and final portions of one or more quarters of a verse. (VKal 4.1.2)
The foot, the beginning, middle, and end portions of a single foot,
and those same positions within multiple feet.
An example of *pādayamaka* (foot-parallelism) is as follows:
For one whose speech toward the wicked is like the honey of a flower yet is censured, there shall be the honey of a flower from that very tree of poison, which is likewise censured.
Examples of *yamaka* (repetition) at the beginning, middle, and end of a single line are as follows:
"O slayer of enemies, O wise one, praised by the wise!
May the policy of Kāmandakī, which is so full of desire, be enjoyed by you day and night."

As those women, like lifeless corpses, cast aside their beloved—who was unblemished, possessed the luster of the spotless moon, self-controlled, and yet rendered powerless—what relish can there be for them? It is as if one were seeking it in grains of sand.

O Sudṛśā, your glance is measured and steady, yet it is startled by the thrill of passion; even a mere fragment of your smile, like a cluster of blossoms, surely outweighs the sweetness of the God of Love himself.
Examples of *yamaka* (repetition) at the beginning, middle, and end of the two feet: O bee (*bhramara*), wander (*bhrama*) while drinking the honey from the flowers in full bloom!
What pleasure is there in the *kunda* blossom that you cry out with such a plaintive tone (*kāku*)?
The unbearable sorrow she bestowed within her heart was like the flowing tears of Vāhīka women streaming down their cheeks.

O, how strange! As soon as a person is initiated by one who has been initiated into the reality of Smara (Kāma) and is pure with smiles, they become possessed of a mind—alas, it is certainly not a false claim, for how could there be a burning of the mind?
An example of *yamaka* at the end of every other quarter-verse (*pāda*) is as follows:
"The poor governance of that king causes living beings to tremble;
for him who is deprived of the lion-throne, his wretched rule will soon come to an end."
In this manner, these internal *yamakas* at the beginning and middle of the quarters are to be inferred.
An example of a *yamaka* at the end of all four quarters is as follows:
"Beholding that slender woman, whose face was as lovely as the moon, who performed a firm dance with the movement of her arched and elevated brows..."
O mind, why do you weary yourself with this fickle woman? If you are a man of action, seek one who is abundant in beauty and whose face is like that of Smara’s command.
In this manner, all types of *yamakas*—beginning with those at the start of a quarter-verse and those in the middle—are to be explained.
Other varieties arising from combinations [of these types] should be discerned by the wise.
As for *akṣarayamaka*, it consists of both single syllables and multiple syllables.
As for the single syllable (ekākṣara), for example:
"The youth, whose mind was won over by the lovely-browed woman through various gestures,
carved the hearts of men with his secluded dalliance."
This should also be understood to apply when there is a connection with other locations.
Its excellence arises from its being born together and its continuity;
and this is seen in the *Hariprabodha*, as follows:
With various white forests, with elephants increasing their strength, with the sky made vast, with people sinking [in the water],
with deer, rabbits, and women, with boats making a humming sound, for me whose body is benefited by the sounds from their mouths.
And by this garland of syllable-yamakas, the garland of verse-yamakas is explained. //2//
From dissolution comes excellence.
Indeed, the most excellent *yamaka* arises from the analysis of its constituent parts. //3//
The chain, the turner, and the powder—this is the path of breaking.
Indeed, these varieties beginning with *śṛṅkhalā* constitute the types of *yamaka-bhaṅga*. //4//
He explains them in sequence:
"The separation of syllables and the movement [of the breath] constitute the *śṛṅkhalā*."
The separation of syllables is *varṇaviccheda*.
The shifting of that [separation] is what constitutes a *śṛṅkhalā*.
For example—in the word *kālikāmadhu*—there is a shifting of the separation of the word *kāma* and the separation of the word *madhu*.
Because of the separation between the *li* and *ma* vowels. //5//
Upon the cessation of attachment, the attainment of one's true nature is transformation.
*Saṅga* is the contact with another color;
when that ceases, the attainment (*prāpti*) of the inherent form—which had been obscured by the other color—is *parivartaka*. For example:
"The honey of the bud is censured."
In this case, the word *arhitam* has acquired another form, *garhitam*, due to its contact with the consonant *ga*.
When that contact with the consonant ceases, it returns to its own original form—namely, *arhitam*.
The intended meaning is that this is a rule for restoring the original form of a word whose shape has been altered through the transition to another phoneme.
By this, the other two [reasons] are also explained. //6//
When there is a division of the *piṇḍa* and the syllables, the loss of its own form is *cūrṇa*.

When there is a division of the syllable-cluster (piṇḍākṣara), the disappearance of the essential form of the word is "powder" (cūrṇa). For example: "The movement of the arrangement of indivisible syllables is stainless like a chain.
Indeed, by this variety of structural breaks, there is a manifoldness of *yamaka* (rhyme) figures.
When, having abandoned association with anything else, one ascends to the very nature of sound— just as a dancer discards his costume— that should be known as *parivartaka*.
When, through the division of a syllable-cluster (piṇḍākṣara) based on its preceding and following words,
there is an elision of two phonemes (varṇa) from a word, that is a "break" (bhaṅga) known as *cūrṇa*.
Though they remain in their proper places, these yamakas do not shine excessively, like locks of hair that have not yet been powdered and curled.
Those who are experts in the excellence of *yamaka* do not accept as such a *yamaka* where there might be a disruption caused by the alteration of case endings.
However,
if a verse that has ascended to a high level of the art of *yamaka* (paronomasia) should be flawed, then the application of *anuprāsa* (alliteration) to it is no longer appropriate.

The distinctness of case-endings, as well as that of number and grammatical function, and the repetition of words ending in *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes with one another, produce the wonder of *yamaka* (chiasmus). //7//
The *anuprāsa* (alliteration) consisting of the remainder is that which possesses similar form.

"Simile is the similarity of the object of comparison (*upameya*) with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), based on even a slight degree of shared quality. (VKal 4.2.1)
That by which something else is compared—that is, brought into a state of similarity—on account of its superior qualities, is the *upamāna* (standard of comparison).
That which is compared, possessing inferior qualities, is the *upameya* (the object of comparison).
The similarity between the *upameya* and the *upamāna* based on even a slight degree of shared quality is what constitutes *upamā* (simile).
Now, "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) and "object of comparison" (*upameya*) are indeed relative terms; by the mention of either one, the other is necessarily established.
For instance, in the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge*, the term *upamitam* alone was employed.
"Just as there is no mention of the comparison," so too here,

True.
That was done for the purpose of adopting what is well-known in the world;

For it is not the case that [one would say], "The face is like a lotus," [if it were not so known].
Likewise, there is also the expression "like a water-lily" (kumudam iva). //1//
And it is designated [as such] on account of the abundance of its qualities. // VKal_4,2.2 //
The abundance of qualities is *guṇabāhulya*;
from that, because of the similarity between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), it is a "conceived simile" (*kalpitopamā*).
It is called "conceived" (*kalpitā*) because it is fashioned by poets.
But the former [comparison] is worldly.

Now, one might object: since there is no worldly consensus regarding that which is purely imaginary, how can there be a fixed rule for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*)? [The answer is:

The orb of the moon, resembling the impression left upon the high, pressed-down breasts of a young Hūṇa maiden during the amorous play of coitus,

That twofold nature [of simile] arises from the distinction between its occurrence in the meaning of a word (*pada*) and the meaning of a sentence (*vākya*).
(VKal 4.2.3) That is, there is a twofold nature of that simile.
This is due to the distinction between the functions of word-meaning and sentence-meaning:
one is the function of word-meaning, while the other is the function of sentence-meaning.
An example of a function based on the meaning of words (padārthavṛtti) is as follows:
"On those [women] whose bodies were green and from whom the tawny skin had been removed, there appeared a downy growth resembling a particle of gold, born of the god of love."
An example of the function of the sentence-meaning (vākyārthavṛtti) is as follows:

"This Pāṇḍya king, with a long necklace resting on his shoulder and his body anointed with yellow sandalwood paste, shines like the King of Mountains, whose peaks are reddened by the morning sun and from which mountain torrents are gushing forth. (3)
That [offering] is both full and deficient.
That simile is both complete and elliptical. //4//
The complete simile occurs when there is the assemblage of words expressing the quality, the standard of comparison, and the object of comparison.
The *pūrṇā* [type of simile] occurs when words such as *guṇa* (quality) and so forth denote the totality or completeness [of the qualities]. For example:
"This face is as charming as a lotus. //5//
When there is an elision, it is called *luptā*.

*Luptā* occurs when there is an absence or elision of words such as those expressing qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. For example, when a word expressing a quality is elided, as in "the king is like the moon" (*śaśīva rājā*).
When an indicative word (*dyotaka*) is elided, as in "this [woman] is dark-green like dūrvā grass" (*dūrvāśyāmeyam*).
An example of the elision of both [the object of comparison and the common attribute] is "śaśīmukhī" (she whose face is like the moon).
The elision of both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, however, is to be seen in the detailed exposition of similes (*upamāprapañca*). //6//
In the explanations of praise, blame, and reality.
Its employment occurs in praise, in censure, and in the statement of reality. As for praise and censure, for example:
"Oh, what a wife! She is affectionate, abundant, and like nectar."
That very thing is devoid of merit, like the *hālāhala* poison;
as it is stated in the *Tattvākhyāna*:
"Know her to be Rohiṇī here within this circle of luminaries."

The defects of that [comparison] are inferiority, superiority, difference of gender and number, dissimilarity, and impossibility. // VKal_4.2.8 //
The defects of that simile are:
inferiority, superiority, difference of gender, difference of number, dissimilarity, and impossibility. //8//
To explain these in sequence, he says: "Deficiency of the simile consists in the inferiority of its genus, measure, or quality. (VKal_4.2.9)

The inferiority of a comparison in terms of genus (*jāti*), measure (*pramāṇa*), or quality (*dharma*) constitutes its deficiency (*hīnatva*). An example of deficiency in the form of inferiority of genus is as follows:
"A supreme act of violence has been committed by you, just like [the acts] of *caṇḍālas*."
Inferiority in the form of deficiency in magnitude is as follows:
"This sun shines like a spark of fire.
That which is the inferiority of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) relative to the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is "inferiority of attributes" (*dharmanyanatva*).
Such was his humble appearance— as follows: marked by the girdle of muñja grass and wearing a garment of black antelope skin, that sage shone like the sun embraced by a portion of dark clouds.
In this case, there is inferiority because the lightning, which is the counterpart to the girdle (*mauñjī*), does not exist as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Furthermore, it is not appropriate for the mere black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina-paṭa*) alone to be the object of comparison,
as that would result in the girdle being rendered purposeless.
[Objection: Is it not the case that lightning is understood by the very mention of the dark cloud?
[Reply: No, because of the possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra). //9//
But when there is no deviation, by what can the resulting cognition be prevented? To this he says:
"When one of two properties is mentioned, there is the cognition of the other due to their association. (VKal 4.2.10)
When even one of two phenomena is explained, there arises a cognition and understanding of the other.
Why?
Because of their constant association (sāhacarya).
When two things are well known to be associated, the mention of one necessarily brings about the cognition of the other. For example:
"Even when the external wealth has ceased, the drops of milk—tawny like honey-drops and cutting through the web of spider-silk within the old house—do not stop."
Having fallen upon the child's topknot in the form of lint, they cause pain to the heart of the housewife, whose sleep has been shattered by the tossing of the infant's limbs.
In this context, roundness and tawny color are co-occurring attributes of honey-drops (*madhupṛṣata*).
Therein, once tawny color is understood through the word "tawny" (*piṅga*), the cognition of roundness arises.
By this, the description "the square reflection of a row [of drops] on a golden surface" is explained.
Because of the constant association (*sāhacarya*) between the golden surface and its whiteness and squareness, the whiteness is understood through the very mention of squareness.
Now, if a deficiency in attributes (*dharmanyūnatva*) is a defect of the analogy (*upamāna*), how is this the following formulation?—

When the eyes of the wretched peacocks were closed by the rays of the sun and they lay down due to the exhaustion caused by the wind, the cries from their mouths vanished, like virtuous wives separated from their husbands within their own homes.
Here, the plurality [of the object of comparison] arises from the attributes of the object of comparison being distinct from the standard of comparison;

this is not so, because it is only specific faces that constitute the objects of comparison, since the destruction of the *kekā* (the cry of a peacock) is possible only in relation to such [specific] things. //10//
By this, the case of *adhikaraṇa* has been explained.
By that, superiority is explained through inferiority.
Superiority consists in the excellence of genus, measure, and quality (*jāti-pramāṇa-dharma*).
An example of superiority in the form of excellence of genus is as follows:
Let the attendants enter swiftly, like Rudras of great majesty; her form is of superlative proportions:
her navel is like the netherworld (pātāla), and her breasts resemble the mountains of the earth.
